024/**
025 * A particle filter estimates the state of a system by representing the state distribution with a
026 * set of weighted samples called particles. Unlike Kalman filters, it doesn't assume the state
027 * distribution is Gaussian, so it can handle strongly nonlinear models and multimodal
028 * distributions.
029 *
030 * <p>Each prediction step propagates every particle through the dynamics model and adds sampled
031 * process noise. Each correction step reweights the particles by the likelihood of the measurement
032 * given each particle, then resamples the particles if too few of them carry most of the weight.
033 *
034 * <p>The state estimate x-hat is the weighted mean of the particles, and the error covariance P is
035 * their weighted sample covariance.
036 *
037 * <p>The filter's computational cost is proportional to the number of particles. More particles
038 * give a more accurate approximation of the state distribution.
039 *
040 * <p>This class implements the generic particle filter in [2, Algorithm 3, p. 180] with the
041 * dynamics model as the importance density [2, eq. (62), p. 179]. That importance density comes
042 * from the bootstrap filter [1, Section 3.1, p. 108], also known as the sampling importance
043 * resampling (SIR) filter [2, Section V-B1, p. 181]. Unlike those filters, this one only resamples
044 * when the effective sample size is low instead of every timestep.
045 *
046 * <p>As shown in [2, eq. (49), p. 178], the N particles xᵢ with weights Wᵢ approximate the
047 * posterior state distribution as
048 *
049 * <pre>
050 *   p(xₖ | y₁, …, yₖ) ≈ Σᵢ Wᵢ δ(xₖ − xᵢ)
051 * </pre>
052 *
053 * <p>where δ is the Dirac delta and Σᵢ Wᵢ = 1.
054 *
055 * <p>References:
056 *
057 * <p>[1] N. J. Gordon, D. J. Salmond, and A. F. M. Smith, "Novel approach to nonlinear/non-Gaussian
058 * Bayesian state estimation," IEE Proceedings F, vol. 140, no. 2, pp. 107–113, 1993. DOI:
059 * 10.1049/ip-f-2.1993.0015 <a
060 * href="https://www.ece.iastate.edu/~namrata/EE520/Gordonnovelapproach.pdf">https://www.ece.iastate.edu/~namrata/EE520/Gordonnovelapproach.pdf</a>
061 *
062 * <p>[2] M. S. Arulampalam, S. Maskell, N. Gordon, and T. Clapp, "A tutorial on particle filters
063 * for online nonlinear/non-Gaussian Bayesian tracking," IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing,
064 * vol. 50, no. 2, pp. 174–188, 2002. DOI: 10.1109/78.978374 <a
065 * href="https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~pabbeel/cs287-fa12/optreadings/Arulampalam_etal_2002.pdf">https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~pabbeel/cs287-fa12/optreadings/Arulampalam_etal_2002.pdf</a>
066 *
067 * <p>[3] R. Douc, O. Cappé, and E. Moulines, "Comparison of resampling schemes for particle
068 * filtering," Proceedings of the 4th International Symposium on Image and Signal Processing and
069 * Analysis (ISPA), pp. 64–69, 2005. <a
070 * href="https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0507025">https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0507025</a>
071 *
072 * @param <States> Number of states.
073 * @param <Inputs> Number of inputs.
074 * @param <Outputs> Number of outputs.
075 */
076public class ParticleFilter<States extends Num, Inputs extends Num, Outputs extends Num>
077    implements KalmanTypeFilter<States, Inputs, Outputs> {
078  // [1] uses our notation except their particle weights qᵢ are our Wᵢ.
079  // [2]'s z, v, n, and wₖⁱ are our y, w, v, and Wᵢ respectively
080  // (measurements, process noise, measurement noise, and particle weights).
081
082  private final Nat<States> m_states;
083  private final Nat<Outputs> m_outputs;
084
085  private final BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<Inputs, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>> m_f;
086  private final BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<Inputs, N1>, Matrix<Outputs, N1>> m_h;
087  private final BiFunction<Matrix<States, ?>, Matrix<?, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>> m_meanFuncX;
088  private final BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>>
089      m_residualFuncX;
090  private final BiFunction<Matrix<Outputs, N1>, Matrix<Outputs, N1>, Matrix<Outputs, N1>>
091      m_residualFuncY;
092  private final BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>> m_addFuncX;
093
094  // Each column is one particle
095  private SimpleMatrix m_particles;
096
097  // Column vector of particle weights
098  private final SimpleMatrix m_weights;
099
100  // Scratch storage for resampling, preallocated to reduce garbage
101  private SimpleMatrix m_resampled;
102
103  private Matrix<States, N1> m_xHat;
104  private Matrix<States, States> m_P;
105
106  private final Matrix<States, N1> m_contStateStdDevs;
107  private final Matrix<Outputs, Outputs> m_contR;
108  private double m_dt;
109
110  private final Random m_random = new Random();
111
112  /**
113   * Constructs a particle filter.
114   *
115   * <p>All particles start at the zero state, so the initial error covariance is zero. Call
116   * setXhat() and setP() to set the initial state distribution.
117   *
118   * <p>See <a
119   * href="https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/state-space/state-space-observers.html#process-and-measurement-noise-covariance-matrices">https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/state-space/state-space-observers.html#process-and-measurement-noise-covariance-matrices</a>
120   * for how to select the standard deviations.
121   *
122   * @param states A Nat representing the number of states.
123   * @param outputs A Nat representing the number of outputs.
124   * @param f A vector-valued function of x and u that returns the derivative of the state vector.
125   * @param h A vector-valued function of x and u that returns the measurement vector.
126   * @param stateStdDevs Standard deviations of model states.
127   * @param measurementStdDevs Standard deviations of measurements.
128   * @param numParticles Number of particles. Must be positive.
129   * @param dt Nominal discretization timestep in seconds.
130   * @throws IllegalArgumentException if numParticles isn't positive.
131   */
132  public ParticleFilter(
133      Nat<States> states,
134      Nat<Outputs> outputs,
135      BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<Inputs, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>> f,
136      BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<Inputs, N1>, Matrix<Outputs, N1>> h,
137      Matrix<States, N1> stateStdDevs,
138      Matrix<Outputs, N1> measurementStdDevs,
139      int numParticles,
140      double dt) {
141    this(
142        states,
143        outputs,
144        f,
145        h,
146        stateStdDevs,
147        measurementStdDevs,
148        (particles, weights) -> particles.times(Matrix.changeBoundsUnchecked(weights)),
149        Matrix::minus,
150        Matrix::minus,
151        Matrix::plus,
152        numParticles,
153        dt);
154  }
155
156  /**
157   * Constructs a particle filter with custom mean, residual, and addition functions. Using custom
158   * functions for arithmetic can be useful if you have angles in the state or measurements, because
159   * they allow you to correctly account for the modular nature of angle arithmetic (see
160   * AngleStatistics.angleMean(), AngleStatistics.angleResidual(), and AngleStatistics.angleAdd()).
161   *
162   * <p>All particles start at the zero state, so the initial error covariance is zero. Call
163   * setXhat() and setP() to set the initial state distribution.
164   *
165   * <p>See <a
166   * href="https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/state-space/state-space-observers.html#process-and-measurement-noise-covariance-matrices">https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/state-space/state-space-observers.html#process-and-measurement-noise-covariance-matrices</a>
167   * for how to select the standard deviations.
168   *
169   * @param states A Nat representing the number of states.
170   * @param outputs A Nat representing the number of outputs.
171   * @param f A vector-valued function of x and u that returns the derivative of the state vector.
172   * @param h A vector-valued function of x and u that returns the measurement vector.
173   * @param stateStdDevs Standard deviations of model states.
174   * @param measurementStdDevs Standard deviations of measurements.
175   * @param meanFuncX A function that computes the weighted mean of the particles (one particle per
176   *     column) given a column vector of weights that sum to one.
177   * @param residualFuncX A function that computes the residual of two state vectors (i.e. it
178   *     subtracts them.)
179   * @param residualFuncY A function that computes the residual of two measurement vectors (i.e. it
180   *     subtracts them.)
181   * @param addFuncX A function that adds two state vectors.
182   * @param numParticles Number of particles. Must be positive.
183   * @param dt Nominal discretization timestep in seconds.
184   * @throws IllegalArgumentException if numParticles isn't positive.
185   */
186  public ParticleFilter(
187      Nat<States> states,
188      Nat<Outputs> outputs,
189      BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<Inputs, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>> f,
190      BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<Inputs, N1>, Matrix<Outputs, N1>> h,
191      Matrix<States, N1> stateStdDevs,
192      Matrix<Outputs, N1> measurementStdDevs,
193      BiFunction<Matrix<States, ?>, Matrix<?, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>> meanFuncX,
194      BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>> residualFuncX,
195      BiFunction<Matrix<Outputs, N1>, Matrix<Outputs, N1>, Matrix<Outputs, N1>> residualFuncY,
196      BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<States, N1>> addFuncX,
197      int numParticles,
198      double dt) {
199    if (numParticles <= 0) {
200      throw new IllegalArgumentException("ParticleFilter numParticles must be positive");
201    }
202
203    m_states = states;
204    m_outputs = outputs;
205
206    m_f = f;
207    m_h = h;
208    m_meanFuncX = meanFuncX;
209    m_residualFuncX = residualFuncX;
210    m_residualFuncY = residualFuncY;
211    m_addFuncX = addFuncX;
212
213    m_contStateStdDevs = stateStdDevs.copy();
214    m_contR = StateSpaceUtil.covarianceMatrix(outputs, measurementStdDevs);
215    m_dt = dt;
216
217    m_particles = new SimpleMatrix(states.getNum(), numParticles);
218    m_weights = new SimpleMatrix(numParticles, 1);
219    m_weights.fill(1.0 / numParticles);
220    m_resampled = new SimpleMatrix(states.getNum(), numParticles);
221
222    updateStatistics();
223
224    UsageReporting.reportUsage("ParticleFilter", "");
225  }
226
227  /**
228   * Returns the error covariance matrix P, which is the weighted sample covariance of the
229   * particles.
230   *
231   * @return The error covariance matrix P.
232   */
233  @Override
234  public Matrix<States, States> getP() {
235    return m_P;
236  }
237
238  /**
239   * Returns an element of the error covariance matrix P.
240   *
241   * @param row Row of P.
242   * @param col Column of P.
243   * @return The value of the error covariance matrix P at (i, j).
244   */
245  @Override
246  public double getP(int row, int col) {
247    return m_P.get(row, col);
248  }
249
250  /**
251   * Sets the error covariance matrix P by redrawing the particles from a Gaussian distribution
252   * centered on the current state estimate x-hat with covariance P.
253   *
254   * @param newP The error covariance matrix P. Must be symmetric positive semidefinite.
255   */
256  @Override
257  public void setP(Matrix<States, States> newP) {
258    // Draw each particle as
259    //
260    //   xᵢ = x̂ + Sεᵢ
261    //
262    // where εᵢ ~ N(0, I) and SSᵀ = P. Then
263    //
264    //   Cov(Sεᵢ) = S E[εᵢεᵢᵀ] Sᵀ = SISᵀ = P
265    //
266    // so xᵢ ~ N(x̂, P).
267    final var xHat = m_xHat;
268    final var S = covarianceSqrt(newP);
269    for (int i = 0; i < getNumParticles(); ++i) {
270      setParticle(i, m_addFuncX.apply(xHat, S.times(sampleStandardNormal())));
271    }
272    m_weights.fill(1.0 / getNumParticles());
273    updateStatistics();
274  }
275
276  /**
277   * Returns the state estimate x-hat, which is the weighted mean of the particles.
278   *
279   * @return The state estimate x-hat.
280   */
281  @Override
282  public Matrix<States, N1> getXhat() {
283    return m_xHat;
284  }
285
286  /**
287   * Returns an element of the state estimate x-hat.
288   *
289   * @param row Row of x-hat.
290   * @return The value of the state estimate x-hat at that row.
291   */
292  @Override
293  public double getXhat(int row) {
294    return m_xHat.get(row, 0);
295  }
296
297  /**
298   * Sets the state estimate x-hat by shifting every particle by the same amount. This preserves the
299   * shape of the state distribution.
300   *
301   * @param xHat The state estimate x-hat.
302   */
303  @Override
304  public void setXhat(Matrix<States, N1> xHat) {
305    // Shift every particle by δ = x̂′ − x̂, where x̂′ is the new state estimate:
306    //
307    //   xᵢ ← xᵢ + δ
308    //
309    // With the default arithmetic, the new mean is Σᵢ Wᵢ(xᵢ + δ) = x̂ + δ = x̂′,
310    // and each residual (xᵢ + δ) − (x̂ + δ) = xᵢ − x̂ is unchanged, so P is
311    // unchanged.
312    final var delta = m_residualFuncX.apply(xHat, m_xHat);
313    for (int i = 0; i < getNumParticles(); ++i) {
314      setParticle(i, m_addFuncX.apply(getParticle(i), delta));
315    }
316    updateStatistics();
317  }
318
319  /**
320   * Sets an element of the state estimate x-hat by shifting every particle by the same amount. This
321   * preserves the shape of the state distribution.
322   *
323   * @param row Row of x-hat.
324   * @param value Value for element of x-hat.
325   */
326  @Override
327  public void setXhat(int row, double value) {
328    final var xHat = m_xHat.copy();
329    xHat.set(row, 0, value);
330    setXhat(xHat);
331  }
332
333  /** Resets the observer. All particles are moved to the zero state and given equal weights. */
334  @Override
335  public final void reset() {
336    m_particles.zero();
337    m_weights.fill(1.0 / getNumParticles());
338    updateStatistics();
339  }

368  /**
369   * Seeds the random number generator used for process noise and resampling. This makes the
370   * filter's output reproducible.
371   *
372   * @param seed The seed.
373   */
374  public void setSeed(long seed) {
375    m_random.setSeed(seed);
376  }
377
378  /**
379   * Project the model into the future with a new control input u.
380   *
381   * @param u New control input from controller.
382   * @param dt Timestep for prediction in seconds.
383   */
384  @Override
385  public void predict(Matrix<Inputs, N1> u, double dt) {
386    // Sample each particle from the dynamics model [1, Section 3.1, p. 108]
387    // [2, Section V-B1, p. 181]:
388    //
389    //   xᵢ ← RK4(f, xᵢ, u, dt) + wᵢ,  wᵢ ~ N(0, Q_d)
390    //
391    // Because the importance density is the dynamics model itself, the weight
392    // update only depends on the likelihood [2, eq. (63), p. 179], so the
393    // weights don't change during prediction.
394    //
395    // For dynamics linearized as ẋ = Ax + Bu + w, where w has continuous
396    // process noise covariance Q, the discrete process noise covariance over a
397    // timestep T = dt is
398    //
399    //   Q_d = ∫₀ᵀ e^(Aτ) Q e^(Aᵀτ) dτ
400    //
401    // which Discretization.discretizeAQ() computes exactly. Each particle would
402    // need its own linearization A to use that, so the first-order term is used
403    // instead:
404    //
405    //   Q_d = QT + O(T²)
406    //
407    // Q = diag(σ₁², …, σₙ²) is diagonal, so wᵢ = √T diag(σ) εᵢ with
408    // εᵢ ~ N(0, I) gives Cov(wᵢ) = T diag(σ)² = QT.
409    final var discStdDevs = m_contStateStdDevs.times(Math.sqrt(dt));
410
411    for (int i = 0; i < getNumParticles(); ++i) {
412      final var x = NumericalIntegration.rk4(m_f, getParticle(i), u, dt);
413      setParticle(i, m_addFuncX.apply(x, discStdDevs.elementTimes(sampleStandardNormal())));
414    }
415
416    m_dt = dt;
417
418    updateStatistics();
419  }
420
421  /**
422   * Correct the state estimate x-hat using the measurements in y.
423   *
424   * @param u Same control input used in the predict step.
425   * @param y Measurement vector.
426   */
427  @Override
428  public void correct(Matrix<Inputs, N1> u, Matrix<Outputs, N1> y) {
429    correct(m_outputs, u, y, m_h, m_contR, m_residualFuncY);
430  }
431
432  /**
433   * Correct the state estimate x-hat using the measurements in y.
434   *
435   * <p>This is useful for when the measurement noise covariances vary.
436   *
437   * @param u Same control input used in the predict step.
438   * @param y Measurement vector.
439   * @param R Continuous measurement noise covariance matrix.
440   */
441  public void correct(Matrix<Inputs, N1> u, Matrix<Outputs, N1> y, Matrix<Outputs, Outputs> R) {
442    correct(m_outputs, u, y, m_h, R, m_residualFuncY);
443  }
444
445  /**
446   * Correct the state estimate x-hat using the measurements in y.
447   *
448   * <p>This is useful for when the measurements available during a timestep's correct() call vary.
449   * The h(x, u) passed to the constructor is used if one is not provided (the two-argument version
450   * of this function).
451   *
452   * @param <Rows> Number of rows in the result of h(x, u).
453   * @param rows Number of rows in the result of h(x, u).
454   * @param u Same control input used in the predict step.
455   * @param y Measurement vector.
456   * @param h A vector-valued function of x and u that returns the measurement vector.
457   * @param R Continuous measurement noise covariance matrix.
458   */
459  public <Rows extends Num> void correct(
460      Nat<Rows> rows,
461      Matrix<Inputs, N1> u,
462      Matrix<Rows, N1> y,
463      BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<Inputs, N1>, Matrix<Rows, N1>> h,
464      Matrix<Rows, Rows> R) {
465    correct(rows, u, y, h, R, Matrix::minus);
466  }
467
468  /**
469   * Correct the state estimate x-hat using the measurements in y.
470   *
471   * <p>This is useful for when the measurements available during a timestep's correct() call vary.
472   * The h(x, u) passed to the constructor is used if one is not provided (the two-argument version
473   * of this function).
474   *
475   * @param <Rows> Number of rows in the result of h(x, u).
476   * @param rows Number of rows in the result of h(x, u).
477   * @param u Same control input used in the predict step.
478   * @param y Measurement vector.
479   * @param h A vector-valued function of x and u that returns the measurement vector.
480   * @param R Continuous measurement noise covariance matrix. Must be symmetric positive definite.
481   * @param residualFuncY A function that computes the residual of two measurement vectors (i.e. it
482   *     subtracts them.)
483   */
484  public <Rows extends Num> void correct(
485      Nat<Rows> rows,
486      Matrix<Inputs, N1> u,
487      Matrix<Rows, N1> y,
488      BiFunction<Matrix<States, N1>, Matrix<Inputs, N1>, Matrix<Rows, N1>> h,
489      Matrix<Rows, Rows> R,
490      BiFunction<Matrix<Rows, N1>, Matrix<Rows, N1>, Matrix<Rows, N1>> residualFuncY) {
491    // The general sequential importance sampling weight update is
492    // [2, eq. (48), p. 178]
493    //
494    //   Wᵢ ∝ Wᵢ⁻ p(y | xᵢ) p(xᵢ | xᵢ⁻) / q(xᵢ | xᵢ⁻, y)
495    //
496    // where q is the importance density. predict() samples from the dynamics
497    // model, so q(xᵢ | xᵢ⁻, y) = p(xᵢ | xᵢ⁻) and the update reduces to
498    // [2, eqs. (62)–(63), p. 179]
499    //
500    //   Wᵢ ∝ Wᵢ⁻ p(y | xᵢ)
501    //
502    // With Gaussian measurement noise, the likelihood is
503    //
504    //   p(y | xᵢ) = (2π)^(−m/2) |R_d|^(−½) exp(−½ rᵢᵀR_d⁻¹rᵢ)
505    //
506    // where rᵢ = y − h(xᵢ, u), m is the number of measurements, and
507    // R_d = R/T is the discrete measurement noise covariance from
508    // Discretization.discretizeR(). The leading constant is the same for every
509    // particle, so it cancels during normalization and only
510    // exp(−½ rᵢᵀR_d⁻¹rᵢ) is needed.
511    //
512    // With the Cholesky decomposition R_d = LLᵀ,
513    //
514    //   rᵢᵀR_d⁻¹rᵢ = rᵢᵀL⁻ᵀL⁻¹rᵢ = (L⁻¹rᵢ)ᵀ(L⁻¹rᵢ) = ‖L⁻¹rᵢ‖²
515    //
516    // so a triangular solve replaces the matrix inverse.
517    final double[] L =
518        Discretization.discretizeR(R, m_dt).lltDecompose(true).getStorage().getDDRM().data;
519
520    // Weights are updated in log space to avoid underflow when the likelihoods
521    // are tiny:
522    //
523    //   ℓᵢ = ln Wᵢ⁻ − ½‖L⁻¹rᵢ‖²
524    final int N = getNumParticles();
525    final double[] logWeights = new double[N];
526    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
527      final var r = residualFuncY.apply(y, h.apply(getParticle(i), u));
528
529      // Solve Lz = r in place for z = L⁻¹r
530      final double[] z = r.getData().clone();
531      TriangularSolver_DDRM.solveL(L, z, rows.getNum());
532      double squaredNorm = 0.0;
533      for (double elem : z) {
534        squaredNorm += elem * elem;
535      }
536
537      logWeights[i] = Math.log(m_weights.get(i, 0)) - 0.5 * squaredNorm;
538
539      // Treat particles with invalid measurements as impossible
540      if (Double.isNaN(logWeights[i])) {
541        logWeights[i] = Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY;
542      }
543    }
544
545    double maxLogWeight = Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY;
546    for (double logWeight : logWeights) {
547      maxLogWeight = Math.max(maxLogWeight, logWeight);
548    }
549
550    if (Double.isFinite(maxLogWeight)) {
551      // Normalize with the log-sum-exp trick:
552      //
553      //   Wᵢ = exp(ℓᵢ − ℓₘₐₓ) / Σⱼ exp(ℓⱼ − ℓₘₐₓ)
554      //
555      // The factor exp(−ℓₘₐₓ) cancels between the numerator and denominator,
556      // so this equals exp(ℓᵢ) / Σⱼ exp(ℓⱼ). Subtracting ℓₘₐₓ makes the
557      // largest term one, so the sum is at least one and normalization can't
558      // divide by zero.
559      double sum = 0.0;
560      for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
561        final double weight = Math.exp(logWeights[i] - maxLogWeight);
562        m_weights.set(i, 0, weight);
563        sum += weight;
564      }
565      CommonOps_DDRM.divide(m_weights.getDDRM(), sum);
566    } else {
567      // No particle is consistent with the measurement, so the measurement
568      // carries no usable information. Fall back to equal weights rather than
569      // dividing by zero.
570      m_weights.fill(1.0 / N);
571    }
572
573    // Resample when the estimated effective sample size [2, eq. (51), p. 179]
574    //
575    //   N̂ₑ = 1 / Σᵢ Wᵢ²
576    //
577    // drops below half the particle count [2, Algorithm 3, p. 180]. N̂ₑ ranges
578    // from 1 (all weight on one particle) to N (equal weights). [2] leaves the
579    // threshold as a design choice, and N/2 is a common heuristic.
580    double sumSquaredWeights = 0.0;
581    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
582      sumSquaredWeights += m_weights.get(i, 0) * m_weights.get(i, 0);
583    }
584    final double effectiveSampleSize = 1.0 / sumSquaredWeights;
585    if (effectiveSampleSize < 0.5 * N) {
586      resample();
587    }
588
589    updateStatistics();
590  }
591
592  /**
593   * Returns particle i.
594   *
595   * @param i The particle index.
596   * @return Particle i.
597   */
598  private Matrix<States, N1> getParticle(int i) {
599    return new Matrix<>(m_particles.extractVector(false, i));
600  }
601
602  /**
603   * Sets particle i.
604   *
605   * @param i The particle index.
606   * @param x The particle's new state.
607   */
608  private void setParticle(int i, Matrix<States, N1> x) {
609    m_particles.insertIntoThis(0, i, x.getStorage());
610  }

612  /**
613   * Returns a vector of independent standard normal samples.
614   *
615   * @return A vector of independent standard normal samples.
616   */
617  private Matrix<States, N1> sampleStandardNormal() {
618    final var epsilon = new Matrix<>(m_states, Nat.N1());
619    for (int i = 0; i < m_states.getNum(); ++i) {
620      epsilon.set(i, 0, m_random.nextGaussian());
621    }
622    return epsilon;
623  }
624
625  /**
626   * Returns S such that SSᵀ = P for a symmetric positive semidefinite P.
627   *
628   * @param P A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix.
629   * @return S such that SSᵀ = P.
630   */
631  private Matrix<States, States> covarianceSqrt(Matrix<States, States> P) {
632    // EJML doesn't have a pivoted LDLT decomposition, and its Cholesky
633    // decomposition fails for singular covariances, so use the symmetric
634    // eigendecomposition instead.
635    //
636    // P = SSᵀ = VΛVᵀ
637    // S = V√(Λ)
638    //
639    // where V's columns are P's orthonormal eigenvectors and Λ is the diagonal
640    // matrix of P's eigenvalues. Λ is clamped to be nonnegative to absorb
641    // roundoff in nearly singular covariances.
642    final int n = m_states.getNum();
643    final EigenDecomposition_F64<DMatrixRMaj> eig = DecompositionFactory_DDRM.eig(n, true, true);
644    if (!eig.decompose(P.getStorage().getDDRM().copy())) {
645      throw new IllegalArgumentException("Eigendecomposition of P failed:\n" + P);
646    }
647
648    final var S = new Matrix<>(m_states, m_states);
649    for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) {
650      final double sqrtLambda = Math.sqrt(Math.max(eig.getEigenvalue(j).getReal(), 0.0));
651      final DMatrixRMaj v = eig.getEigenVector(j);
652      for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
653        S.set(i, j, v.get(i, 0) * sqrtLambda);
654      }
655    }
656    return S;
657  }
658
659  /**
660   * Resamples the particles in proportion to their weights, then resets the weights to be equal.
661   */
662  private void resample() {
663    // Use systematic resampling [2, Algorithm 2, p. 180] [3, Section 2.4],
664    // which draws one uniform random offset, then selects particles at evenly
665    // spaced points along the cumulative weight distribution. It runs in O(N)
666    // time and needs only one random number.
667    //
668    // Residual and stratified resampling are proven to have lower conditional
669    // variance than multinomial resampling [3, Sections 3.2–3.3], but
670    // systematic resampling isn't in general [3, Section 3.4]. Systematic
671    // resampling is still widely used because it's simple and its empirical
672    // performance is generally close to residual and stratified resampling
673    // [3, Section 1].
674    //
675    // With the cumulative weights Cᵢ = W₀ + ⋯ + Wᵢ and C₋₁ = 0, draw
676    //
677    //   U ~ Uniform[0, 1/N)
678    //   uⱼ = U + j/N,  j = 0, …, N − 1
679    //
680    // and select particle i for each uⱼ where C₍ᵢ₋₁₎ < uⱼ ≤ Cᵢ. Each uⱼ is
681    // uniform over a width-1/N interval, so particle i is selected NWᵢ times in
682    // expectation and the resampled set is an unbiased estimate of the weighted
683    // one.
684    final int N = getNumParticles();
685    final double step = 1.0 / N;
686    double position = m_random.nextDouble() * step;
687
688    int i = 0;
689    double cumulativeWeight = m_weights.get(0, 0);
690    for (int j = 0; j < N; ++j) {
691      // Roundoff can leave the total cumulative weight slightly below one, so
692      // stop at the last particle
693      while (position > cumulativeWeight && i < N - 1) {
694        ++i;
695        cumulativeWeight += m_weights.get(i, 0);
696      }
697      m_resampled.insertIntoThis(0, j, m_particles.extractVector(false, i));
698      position += step;
699    }
700
701    final var temp = m_particles;
702    m_particles = m_resampled;
703    m_resampled = temp;
704    m_weights.fill(step);
705  }
706
707  /** Recomputes the state estimate and error covariance from the particles. */
708  private void updateStatistics() {
709    // With the default arithmetic, these are the mean and covariance of the
710    // weighted particle approximation of the posterior:
711    //
712    //   x̂ = Σᵢ Wᵢxᵢ
713    //   P = Σᵢ Wᵢ(xᵢ − x̂)(xᵢ − x̂)ᵀ
714    //
715    // P has no small-sample bias correction. With equal weights, P is
716    // (N − 1)/N times the unbiased sample covariance, which is negligible for
717    // typical particle counts.
718    m_xHat = m_meanFuncX.apply(new Matrix<>(m_particles), new Matrix<>(m_weights));
719
720    final var P = new Matrix<>(m_states, m_states);
721    for (int i = 0; i < getNumParticles(); ++i) {
722      final var r = m_residualFuncX.apply(getParticle(i), m_xHat);
723      final double weight = m_weights.get(i, 0);
724      for (int row = 0; row < m_states.getNum(); ++row) {
725        for (int col = 0; col < m_states.getNum(); ++col) {
726          P.set(row, col, P.get(row, col) + weight * r.get(row, 0) * r.get(col, 0));
727        }
728      }
729    }
730    m_P = P;
731  }
732}
